title: Connecting the Data Center
summary: Design a connected path that considers internal organization, external links, and resilience.
objectives: Distinguish internal connections from external connectivity.
Explain why organized or multiple network paths can improve a design.

vocab.def: How much work, information, or resource a system can handle.
The route information follows between connected systems.
The ability of systems or places to connect and communicate.

sections.heading: A powerful facility needs connections
sections.body: Inside, servers connect to switches and other systems. Outside, fiber and network links connect the facility to buildings, regions, and services. Without useful connectivity, computing capacity has limited reach.

sections.heading: Organize and protect the paths
sections.body: Clear labels and planned cable routes help people understand a system. Multiple conceptual paths can reduce dependence on one connection, but they also require more planning and resources.

sections.heading: Map the information journey
sections.body: Draw a path from an outside network to a switch and then to a server. Add a second path and explain what question it raises. This is design reasoning, not advanced network configuration.

practice.prompt: A design has one external link and two internal links. What single point of failure remains, and what tradeoff might a second external link create?

quiz.question: Why might a design include more than one network path?
options: To reduce dependence on one connection
To eliminate the need for servers
quiz.answer: To reduce dependence on one connection

reflectionPrompt: What makes a network path easy for another person to understand and maintain?
